_comment: Cross-service consistency vectors for the X-Acting-Subject pseudonym. Every service on this contract vendors its own copy and runs the same expected values. What must never diverge is the data below; prose may be rewritten locally.
_notes: The separator is NUL (\u0000), not a colon or a dash -- otherwise (tenant-al, ice) and (tenant-a, lice) collide.
Truncation is on the first 16 bytes of the digest, not the first 16 characters of the hex string. Getting this wrong yields a 16-character value, which a receiver rejects on length.
Output must match ^[0-9a-f]{32}$. Lowercase hex is a subset of every identity character class on this contract, which is why receivers do not have to negotiate their regexes.
tenant_id and subject_id are encoded as UTF-8 before the HMAC. Two vectors below carry non-ASCII subject_ids so that this is exercised rather than assumed.
The salt must be at least 32 bytes. A party that derives with less has implemented the formula but not its strength: the pseudonym still looks correct and no receiver can tell.

The invariant to assert is the canonical payload digest recorded in _payload_sha256, not this file's byte hash -- prose differs between services on purpose. See _payload_canonicalization for how to recompute it.

vectors._why: with the next vector, proves the NUL separator is in effect

non-ASCII subject_id. It pins two things that all-ASCII data leaves invisible: tenant_id and subject_id are encoded as UTF-8 before the HMAC (Latin-1 can represent this character, so a narrower encoding still succeeds and silently yields a different pseudonym), and the ensure_ascii clause of the canonicalisation (with all-ASCII data both settings give the same digest, so that clause sits unguarded until a vector like this one exists). The file itself stays pure ASCII by escaping the character, so services that require ASCII-only sources can still vendor it verbatim.

same subject_id as the first vector under a different tenant_id. Proves the tenant participates in the derivation at all: an implementation that hashed only the subject would still pass every other vector here, and the two services would then hand the same pseudonym to two different organisations' users.
uppercase and punctuation on both halves. Pins that neither half is case-folded or normalised before hashing; a service that lowercased identifiers would collide two distinct subjects.

_payload_canonicalization: Build an object with exactly these keys: header, pseudonym_pattern, min_salt_bytes, vectors.
Each entry of vectors keeps exactly salt, tenant_id, subject_id, expected -- drop _why and anything else.
Serialize with sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True, then SHA-256 the UTF-8 bytes.

ensure_ascii matters even though today's data is all ASCII: the day a vector carries a non-ASCII subject_id, two implementations that disagree on this flag will report a fork while the data is in fact identical -- exactly the false alarm this anchor exists to avoid.
Recomputing this without the rules above is guesswork; a wrong guess reports a fork that is not there.
